name: Confucianism
idea: The Analects do not present life as a test set by a higher intelligence, and Confucius spoke of Heaven (Tian) sparingly; whether Heaven is personal or a moral order is a long-standing question within the tradition. Still, the Analects hold that Heaven knows a person who goes unrecognized, that offending Heaven has no remedy, and that reciprocity is a rule for all of life, including toward those outside one's family. Many Confucians would see in this a call to cultivate character where no one is keeping score.

passages.text: Is not RECIPROCITY such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.
passages.ref: Analects XV.23 (Legge numbering: Book XV, chap. XXIII)
passages.translation: James Legge, The Analects of Confucius (The Chinese Classics), 1893

passages.text: Let the superior man never fail reverentially to order his own conduct, and let him be respectful to others and observant of propriety:-- then all within the four seas will be his brothers.
passages.translation: James Legge, The Analects of Confucius (The Chinese Classics), 1893

passages.text: I do not murmur against Heaven. I do not grumble against men. My studies lie low, and my penetration rises high. But there is Heaven;-- that knows me!
passages.translation: James Legge, The Analects of Confucius (The Chinese Classics), 1893

passages.text: He who offends against Heaven has none to whom he can pray.
passages.translation: James Legge, The Analects of Confucius (The Chinese Classics), 1893

practices.how: Before dealing with a stranger, practice shu: ask what you would want done to you in their place, then do that.
Choose one small matter no one will check, such as returning something extra or keeping a rule, and do it rightly.
Following Analects 12.5, greet and help one stranger this week with the courtesy you would show kin.
Do good work and let it pass without mention. Analects 1.1 asks whether one is not complete in virtue who is not troubled at going unnoticed.
Like Zengzi in Analects 1.4, review your day on a few points, such as whether you were faithful to others and kept your word.

ask: How does our teacher understand Tian today, as a personal observer, a moral order, or both?
How should the Analects' reciprocity be applied to strangers, when so much Confucian teaching begins with family and graded relationships?
What does it mean to act as a junzi when no one is watching, and what practices in our community support that?
caveat: Confucian thinkers differ on whether Heaven is a personal will or an impersonal moral order, and on how far care extends beyond family and community. This guide does not claim Confucianism teaches that life is a test, only that the Analects hold related ideas.
